paragraphs: Clustering is harder when the number of groups is not known in advance. Dirichlet process mixture models address that uncertainty, but their computational demands can make them unsuitable for large datasets. This paper develops deterministic accelerated versions intended to preserve that modeling flexibility while making inference practical at much larger scales.

The method incorporates kd-trees into a variational Bayesian algorithm. These trees provide a structured organization of the data that the algorithm uses to accelerate computation. The underlying mixture uses a stick-breaking representation. The authors also change how truncation is handled: beyond a chosen level, the variational distributions remain fixed at their prior distributions.

The authors report that the resulting methods can routinely process millions of data cases. Their experiments show potentially substantial speedups over the standard variational algorithm. The contribution is therefore a computational route to using flexible mixture models on large datasets, with acceleration coming from both the data structure and the particular treatment of the variational approximation.
neurips-2006-accelerated-variational-dir.tldr: Kd-trees accelerate variational Dirichlet process mixture inference enough to handle millions of data cases.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to distinguish imagined left-hand and right-hand movement from a single EEG trial as quickly and reliably as possible. The relevant activity follows a trigger, but its timing is blurred and the measurements are noisy. A useful classifier therefore needs to accumulate evidence while continuing to produce decisions as new measurements arrive.

The proposed method supplies a probabilistic decision at each time point by combining information from two sequences of features. Earlier decisions contribute through a weighting scheme that gives more emphasis to moments when the feature distributions for the two classes are easier to distinguish. This discriminatory strength is quantified using the Bayes error of misclassification.

The approach was successfully applied in the third BCI competition. Analysis after the data were disclosed supported its reported superiority, with single-trial error rates as low as 10.7%, 11.5%, and 16.7% for the three subjects studied. These findings support weighting accumulated evidence by its discriminatory value in this setting.
neurips-2006-aggregating-classification-.tldr: The method combines EEG evidence over time, emphasizing moments that better distinguish imagined left-hand from right-hand movement.

paragraphs: This paper introduces BART, a Bayesian model that adds together the contributions of multiple decision trees. Each tree is constrained by a prior to act as a weak learner, contributing only a small part of the overall prediction. The model builds on the ensemble idea that several modest predictors can collectively form a strong predictor.

Fitting and inference use an iterative backfitting MCMC procedure. The central distinction from boosting is how the ensemble is specified: BART has an explicit statistical model consisting of a prior and a likelihood. This gives the collection of weak trees a probabilistic foundation for both learning and inference.

The authors report that this formulation supports a full and accurate assessment of predictive uncertainty while retaining highly competitive predictive accuracy. Its importance is that the ensemble produces more than a prediction alone: uncertainty about that prediction is part of the model's output. The paper thus connects weak-tree ensembles with Bayesian assessment of how confidently their predictions should be interpreted.
neurips-2006-bayesian-ensemble-learning-.tldr: BART combines weak decision trees in a Bayesian model that delivers competitive predictions alongside uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Multi-frame super-resolution combines several low-resolution views to estimate a higher-resolution image. A central difficulty is that the alignment between those views is unknown. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that accounts for uncertainty in the registration parameters by integrating over them when reconstructing the image.

The choice of what to integrate over is the key contribution. The earlier Bayesian approach discussed in the abstract integrated over the high-resolution image, which required an unfavorable image prior. Integrating over registration parameters instead permits more realistic image priors and substantially reduces the dimension of the integral, removing the earlier method's main computational bottleneck.

The generative model also includes illumination components alongside motion, allowing changes in lighting to be represented together with changes in alignment. Results on real and synthetic datasets illustrate the approach's effectiveness. The paper shows why the organization of Bayesian inference matters practically: choosing different unknowns to average over can improve both the modeling options and the computational burden.
neurips-2006-bayesian-image-super-resolu.tldr: Integrating over uncertain image alignments makes Bayesian super-resolution more computationally manageable and permits more realistic image priors.

paragraphs: A photograph containing several moving objects can have different amounts of blur in different regions, while other regions remain sharp. The paper addresses recovering such an image when the blur is unknown. Applying one blur kernel to the whole scene can create serious artifacts, so the approach also needs to separate regions according to their blur.

The method uses the observation that blur substantially changes the distributions of image derivatives. Under the stated assumption of constant-velocity motion, the search can be restricted to one-dimensional box-filter blurs. This makes it possible to model the expected derivative distributions as a function of blur-kernel width and use those distributions to distinguish regions.

The authors find that these statistics are powerful indicators of differing blur and report convincing deconvolution results on richly textured real images. The contribution links segmentation and restoration through a shared statistical signal. Its demonstrated effectiveness is tied to the described motion model and image setting, rather than a claim to handle every possible source of blur.
neurips-2006-blind-motion-deblurring-usi.tldr: Image-derivative statistics identify regions with different motion blur, enabling convincing restoration under a constant-velocity motion assumption.

paragraphs: Blind source separation seeks unknown underlying sources from observed signals. This paper focuses on a dimension-reduction setting in which there are more observed signals than sources. The aim is to explain those signals using a small collection of components, while allowing a component to appear at different temporal offsets.

Allowing delays matters for applications such as acoustic signals, muscle measurements, and movement trajectories. Purely linear mixing methods do not provide the required temporal shift invariance. The authors introduce an algorithm based on transforming the generative model into a time-frequency representation using the Wigner-Ville distribution, addressing delayed mixtures specifically in this over-determined setting.

The reported comparisons favor the new algorithm over classical methods for linear mixtures and a related method that handles delays. Applied to human gait trajectories, it also extracts spatial and temporal components that are easier to interpret than those obtained with other classical algorithms. These results connect the method's treatment of timing differences with both separation performance and the interpretability of movement components.
neurips-2006-blind-source-separation-for.tldr: A time-frequency approach separates delayed signal mixtures and extracts interpretable components from human gait trajectories.

paragraphs: When people infer an unfamiliar property of an object, they can draw on more than one kind of knowledge. They may know how properties are related, and they may know how the object resembles other objects. This paper examines how those two sources of knowledge can contribute within a single account of inductive reasoning.

The authors present a Bayesian model that combines relationships between properties with relationships between objects. This brings together information emphasized separately by causal-reasoning models and similarity-based models. The approach matters because a prediction about an object's properties can depend on both its connections to other objects and the connections among the properties themselves.

The model accounts well for human judgments about the properties of biological species. That finding supports the usefulness of combining these forms of knowledge when explaining the studied inferences. The contribution is a unified probabilistic account of reasoning in this domain, showing how causal and similarity information can participate together in the same inference.
neurips-2006-combining-causal-and-simila.tldr: A Bayesian model combines causal relationships between properties with similarity relationships between objects to explain human species-related inferences.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common algorithmic framework for an abstract setting called a convex repeated game. Its purpose is to connect methods that otherwise appear as separate algorithms. In particular, the authors show that various online learning and boosting methods can be obtained as special cases of the same framework.

The mathematical connection links regret in game theory with weak duality in convex optimization. Regret provides a way to assess decisions made over repeated rounds, while duality provides relationships between optimization formulations. Bringing these ideas together supplies the foundation from which the paper's family of algorithms is derived.

The resulting unified view serves two roles: it explains properties of existing methods and supports the derivation of several new algorithms. The contribution is therefore a reusable theoretical structure for understanding algorithm design. Its scope is the online learning and boosting algorithms captured by the framework, with the shared derivation helping reveal why their properties belong to a broader pattern.
neurips-2006-convex-repeated-games-and-f.tldr: A connection between game-theoretic regret and convex duality unifies several online learning and boosting algorithms and yields new ones.

paragraphs: The paper seeks to answer two connected questions from a single image: whether a person is present and how that person's pose can be represented compactly. A useful representation should also allow a new pose image to be compared with examples in a training collection, connecting detection with pose classification and matching.

The authors begin with image descriptors developed for human detection and model their statistics using Latent Dirichlet Allocation. They investigate learning this model without pose labels from images of human poses. The learned structure supplies a low-dimensional description that can support both recognition of human images and comparisons among their poses.

Extensive quantitative experiments and comparisons examine human detection and pose matching. The authors report an effective representation for pose classification and matching, together with strong human-versus-nonhuman decisions. These results support the idea that one statistical model of image features can serve both tasks, so that representing pose contributes to a broader account of what human images look like.
neurips-2006-detecting-humans-via-their-.tldr: An unsupervised feature model learns compact pose representations that also support human detection in single images.

paragraphs: GEM detects anomalies by learning a region associated with nominal, or normal, observations. It is non-parametric, so the proposed detector is built from training-sample geometry. The central idea is to estimate an entropy-minimizing set covering a chosen proportion of the nominal distribution and treat observations outside that set as potential anomalies.

The construction uses entropic graphs containing K points from N training samples. Their stated limiting covering property connects the graph's span to a set containing at least the K/N fraction of the distribution's continuous part. The uncovered fraction determines the statistical significance level associated with declaring an observation anomalous.

For implementation, the authors approximate the target set through a graph's influence region. An incremental leave-one-out nearest-neighbor construction on resampled training subsets enables efficient outlier detection and empirical p-value computation. Examples on simulated and real datasets in high-dimensional feature spaces illustrate the method. The contribution connects a geometric representation of normal data with statistically interpretable anomaly decisions.
neurips-2006-geometric-entropy-minimizat.tldr: GEM uses entropic graphs to estimate normal-data regions and detect outliers with significance levels and empirical p-values.

paragraphs: Finding a low-dimensional representation of high-dimensional data can be formulated as a semidefinite optimization problem. In the setting described here, solutions preserve local distances while favoring high variance or large matrix trace. Such formulations have been observed to produce low-rank solutions naturally, but the original matrix optimization can become very large.

The paper reduces the problem by expressing its solution in terms of the bottom eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian. This produces a matrix factorization that leads to a much smaller semidefinite program. The smaller optimization therefore works within a restricted representation derived from the graph, rather than handling the full original matrix directly.

The authors report that these reduced problems closely approximate the original solutions, with conjugate gradient descent available for further refinement. They illustrate the approach through sensor-network localization, solving optimizations involving tens of thousands of nodes in a few minutes. This demonstrates how a graph-derived representation can make large geometric optimization problems computationally manageable while retaining good approximate solutions.
neurips-2006-graph-laplacian-regularizat.tldr: Graph Laplacian eigenvectors reduce large semidefinite programs to smaller problems that closely approximate their solutions.

paragraphs: The hidden Markov Dirichlet process models genetic inheritance while allowing an unbounded set of ancestral founders. The goal is to explain both recombination between ancestral lineages and sequence changes within lineages. Jointly representing these processes provides an account of the ancestral structure underlying observed haplotypes, or sequences of genetic markers.

At each locus, the model selects an ancestor through a first-order Markov process. Across loci, changes in that selection represent recombination. Combining this process with a mutation model accommodates variation within the resulting genealogies. The authors develop an efficient sampling algorithm based on a two-level nested Polya urn construction to perform inference.

On simulated and real SNP haplotype data, the method performs competitively with or significantly better than existing methods at locating recombination hotspots. It also infers ancestral genetic patterns and produces a reported highly accurate map of ancestral population composition. The findings show the value of treating hotspot detection and ancestral reconstruction as connected outputs of one inheritance model.
neurips-2006-hidden-markov-dirichlet-pro.tldr: An unbounded ancestral-state model jointly represents recombination and mutation to infer hotspots and population ancestry.

paragraphs: The paper addresses anomaly detection in large distributed systems using principal component analysis. The starting approach monitors data projected into a residual subspace for signs of unusual behavior. Although this approach had worked well empirically for highly aggregated networks with relatively few large nodes and coarse time scales, it faced scalability problems.

The proposed detector distributes part of the work across the network. Adaptive filters at local sites control which data reach a coordinator, sending enough information to support accurate global detection. This makes communication itself part of the detector's design: local decisions about reporting data affect what the coordinator can infer about the system.

The method is grounded in a stochastic matrix perturbation analysis that characterizes the relationship between detection accuracy and communication volume. That relationship provides a principled way to understand the consequences of reducing transmitted data. The contribution is a PCA-based distributed architecture whose communication demands and detection accuracy are explicitly connected, addressing a central obstacle to scaling global anomaly monitoring.
neurips-2006-in-network-pca-and-anomaly-.tldr: Adaptive local filters reduce network communication while supporting global PCA anomaly detection through an analyzed accuracy–communication tradeoff.

paragraphs: When several related data sources are available, learning a model for one source raises a selection question: which samples from the other sources should contribute? This paper studies that question for sources that are nearby but distinct. Its inputs include separate samples from each source and estimates of how dissimilar the sources are.

The authors develop a general theory for selecting samples to learn a model for each source. The formulation uses a broad decision-theoretic learning framework, with results covering classification and regression, as well as density estimation within the exponential family. Source relationships therefore inform the choice of training information across several kinds of prediction problems.

A central technical contribution is a collection of approximate triangle inequalities for expected loss. These provide relationships among losses that support the sample-selection theory and may also be useful independently. The paper's significance is its principled treatment of when information from related sources should enter a source-specific model, using dissimilarity estimates as explicit inputs to that reasoning.
neurips-2006-learning-from-multiple-sour.tldr: The paper develops a theory for choosing training samples across related data sources using estimates of their dissimilarity.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a nonlinear generative model of human motion in which observed joint angles are represented by real-valued variables and hidden structure by binary variables. The aim is to capture several kinds of motion within one model, while supporting inference as a motion sequence unfolds over time.

At each time step, the hidden and observed variables form an undirected model. Both also receive directed connections from observed variables in the preceding few time steps. This architecture incorporates recent movement history into the current state. According to the authors, it enables efficient online inference and a simple approximate procedure for learning the model.

After training, a single parameter set captures several different motion types. The authors demonstrate the model by generating motion sequences and filling in missing motion-capture data online. These demonstrations show two uses of the same learned motion structure: synthesizing plausible sequences and reconstructing observations that were lost during capture. The contribution combines temporal conditioning with a shared latent representation of different movements.
neurips-2006-modeling-human-motion-using.tldr: A motion model with binary hidden variables captures multiple movement types and supports sequence generation and online missing-data reconstruction.

paragraphs: Related prediction tasks may benefit from a common compact representation of their inputs. This paper develops a method for learning that representation jointly across tasks. It builds on 1-norm regularization with a new regularizer that controls how many learned features are shared, encouraging the tasks to rely on a limited common feature set.

The authors show that the formulation is equivalent to a convex optimization problem and give an iterative solution method. The algorithm alternates between learning a shared representation in an unsupervised step and learning task-specific prediction functions in a supervised step. This separates what the tasks have in common from how each task uses that common representation.

Experiments on simulated and real data show dramatic improvements relative to learning each task independently. These findings support joint feature learning for the related tasks tested. The same algorithm also includes a simpler special case that selects a few existing features shared across tasks, making the framework applicable to both representation learning and common feature selection.
neurips-2006-multi-task-feature-learning.tldr: A convex formulation learns a small shared feature representation that substantially improves the tested tasks over independent learning.

paragraphs: Changes in movement performance can arise from causes that persist for very different lengths of time. Fatigue can produce relatively fast changes, while disease can produce slower ones. The paper hypothesizes that motor adaptation reflects these temporal differences, with the nervous system responding according to what a movement error suggests about its possible cause.

In the Bayesian formulation, an error creates a credit-assignment problem: which timescale should receive responsibility for the disturbance? The schedule of adaptation influences how an optimal learner answers that question. It changes both estimates associated with different timescales and uncertainty about those estimates, so the pattern of experience affects subsequent adaptation.

A system organized this way predicts many observed properties of saccadic gain adaptation, which concerns adjustment of eye-movement magnitude. It also predicts adaptation time courses under partial sensory deprivation and reversals in adaptation direction. These agreements support the proposed account as an explanation of the studied behavior, while the claim about the nervous system remains a hypothesis.
neurips-2006-multiple-timescales-and-unc.tldr: A Bayesian account of motor adaptation assigns errors to different disturbance timescales and predicts several observed eye-movement adaptation patterns.

paragraphs: The paper studies online classification when each incoming trial contains several connected prediction tasks. Updating the learner must account for those tasks together. The authors formulate the update as a projection problem in which each task contributes a linear constraint, with one shared slack parameter linking the constraints.

Their approximation solves individual projection subproblems independently and simultaneously, then averages the resulting solutions. They show that this produces a feasible solution to the original joint projection problem, although it need not be optimal. This distinction is central: the procedure satisfies the required formulation without claiming to recover its best possible projection.

The authors derive specific simultaneous-projection schemes and analyze their mistakes within the mistake-bound framework. Experiments on online multiclass text categorization indicate that combining class-dependent features with the proposed update method outperforms previously studied algorithms. The contribution connects a manageable approximation of a coupled update problem with theoretical analysis and empirical evidence for the combined approach in text classification.
neurips-2006-online-classification-for-c.tldr: Averaging independent constraint projections gives feasible online classification updates and supports strong results with class-dependent text features.

paragraphs: A neuron can respond to repeated identical fluctuating input currents with highly precise spike timing. This motivates the paper's goal of predicting when a given neuron will fire under a new input current. The authors approach the problem by modeling the membrane potential, the changing electrical state that precedes a spike.

The model mimics the dynamics of that potential and uses its behavior to predict spike occurrence. The key comparison is between thresholding a single instantaneous estimated potential and examining a richer state description before a possible spike. That richer description includes the potential together with its time derivative or derivatives, capturing how the voltage is changing.

The authors find that using this dynamical state significantly improves prediction relative to the instantaneous-threshold approach. The result suggests that information about the trajectory toward a spike adds predictive value beyond voltage level alone. It supports a more dynamic spike-prediction rule, while the stated ambition of handling any input current remains the motivating goal.
neurips-2006-predicting-spike-times-from.tldr: Considering membrane voltage and its changes improves spike-time prediction over thresholding the estimated voltage alone.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the repeated calibration required by machine-learning-based brain-computer interfaces. Even experienced users had to spend roughly 20–30 minutes generating calibration data before their movement intentions could be inferred. The proposed alternative uses information from earlier sessions to avoid collecting a fresh calibration session each time.

The method first defines normalized common spatial pattern features and distances between them. It then constructs representative features across sessions, either by clustering or by feature concatenation. These individualized prototypes provide the basis for a classifier, allowing information from a person's prior sessions to be carried into a new one.

The authors demonstrate successful classifier transfer to a new session for a number of subjects. This supports the possibility of omitting calibration through reuse of earlier session knowledge for those users. The result is specifically about transferring individualized information across sessions: the prototypes preserve a connection to the user's previous data, and the reported success does not establish that calibration can be omitted for every subject.
neurips-2006-reducing-calibration-time-f.tldr: Individualized feature prototypes from earlier BCI sessions enable successful classifier transfer without fresh calibration for several subjects.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a robot can grasp an object that it is seeing for the first time. Its approach predicts a grasp point directly from images, without requiring or constructing a three-dimensional object model. This frames the learning problem around the location needed for the action rather than a complete geometric description.

The algorithm is trained with supervised learning using synthetic images. The learned mapping connects visual input to a predicted point at which the robot should grasp an object. This is significant because the training material is synthetic, while the demonstration tests whether the learned prediction can support physical manipulation of unfamiliar objects.

On a robotic manipulation platform, the approach successfully grasps a wide variety of objects absent from the training set. The examples include wine glasses, duct tape, keys, screwdrivers, toothbrushes, and a thick coil of wire. The demonstration supports direct image-based grasp prediction across the tested objects, showing that useful action locations can be learned without first building explicit three-dimensional models.
neurips-2006-robotic-grasping-of-novel-o.tldr: A robot trained on synthetic images predicts grasp points directly from vision and successfully grasps diverse previously unseen objects.

paragraphs: A controller often has to choose actions using a Markov decision process whose parameters are uncertain. Optimizing only for the worst possible model can produce overly conservative behavior. This paper instead examines the relationship between performance under the nominal model and performance under the worst case among the possible models.

When uncertainty affects only rewards, the authors use parametric linear programming to compute the complete set of Pareto-efficient policies in this two-objective space. These are policies for which improving one objective requires sacrificing the other. The resulting set describes the available compromises, giving a fuller picture than a single worst-case-optimal policy.

The situation changes when transition probabilities are also uncertain. The authors show that a strategy achieving the optimal tradeoff might need to be non-Markovian, so its decisions may depend on more than the current state. The general problem is consequently not tractable. The paper therefore identifies both a computable reward-uncertainty case and a significant difficulty introduced by uncertain dynamics.
neurips-2006-the-robustness-performance-.tldr: The paper computes performance–robustness tradeoffs for uncertain rewards and shows why uncertain transitions make the general problem harder.

paragraphs: An unchanged image can appear to switch between different interpretations during continuous viewing. This paper proposes that such perceptual switching emerges from the brain's search for good interpretations through Bayesian inference. The aim is to explain the dynamics of these switches, rather than simply describe which interpretations an image permits.

The theory assumes a rapid sampling-like exploration of a posterior distribution over possible interpretations. A switch occurs when a sampled alternative has greater value than a discounted version of the current interpretation. This rule connects continued exploration with the persistence and eventual replacement of the interpretation currently being experienced.

The authors formalize the account, derive switching-rate distributions, and examine how changes in the posterior affect switching. Its predictions agree with measured contextual changes in human switching behavior for Necker cube stimuli. This consistency supports the theory as an account of those dynamics, while the proposed sampling process remains a theoretical explanation of how the observed behavior could arise.
neurips-2006-theory-and-dynamics-of-perc.tldr: A Bayesian sampling-like theory explains perceptual switching and predicts contextual changes consistent with Necker cube observations.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks a decomposition into independent components, but its theoretical interpretation depends on the data satisfying its generative assumptions. Independent subspace analysis broadens the idea by allowing dependence within groups while requiring independence between groups. This paper develops a more general formulation that avoids requiring every group to have the same size.

The authors introduce irreducible independent subspaces: components that cannot be further decomposed into independent parts within the formulation. This supports a parameter-free mixture model. They also incorporate earlier non-Gaussian component analysis results to relax the usual restriction allowing at most one Gaussian component, expanding the model's treatment of possible independent structure.

For computation, the paper considers joint block diagonalization with unknown block sizes and builds a simple extension of JADE around it. Simulations confirm the algorithm's feasibility. The contribution connects a broader account of independent subspaces with a concrete computational method, addressing the mismatch between fixed-size groups and the potentially unequal independent structures present in a random vector.
neurips-2006-towards-a-general-independe.tldr: A generalized independent-subspace model removes fixed group-size requirements and motivates a feasible extension of JADE.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to train a conditional random field when the goal is accuracy on individual labels. It adopts empirical risk minimization: choosing model parameters to reduce prediction errors measured on the training set. The relevant error measure is Hamming loss, which evaluates mistakes at the level of separate labels.

The authors provide a gradient-based optimization procedure for an approximation to that empirical risk. The approximation can be made arbitrarily accurate, allowing the training objective to closely track the labelwise error criterion. This directly connects what training seeks to improve with the paper's chosen definition of predictive success.

Experiments using simulated and real data show significantly better test performance than several existing CRF training approaches, especially when label noise is high. These findings support the proposed objective and optimization procedure in the tested settings. The contribution is a practical method for training toward per-label accuracy, with the strongest reported advantage appearing when the supplied labels contain substantial noise.
neurips-2006-training-conditional-random.tldr: Training CRFs with a close approximation to labelwise error improves reported test performance, particularly under high label noise.
